processing: Raw pu-erh handling: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried into maocha, then sold loose or pressed, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: As usual for the area, spring is the prized picking, with lesser summer and autumn lots.
appearance_dry: Varies by mountain; generally dark-green leaves pressed into cakes.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow to golden, as with other young raw teas of the area.
appearance_wet: Supple olive-green leaves whose size varies with the mountain and tree type.
taste_profile: No single flavour for the township. Yibang is described as showy in aroma, and Gedeng as more restrained, with honey and wild flowers and a slight bitterness that fades quickly into a long sweetness.

brewing.notes: Brew in a gaiwan with very hot water and short steeps. Try teas from different mountains side by side, since the township is not one flavour.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually under a mountain name such as Yibang or Gedeng rather than the township, with spring lots most valued. Young cakes are drunk within a few years or stored longer as raw pu-erh typically is.
description:
Xiangming is a Yi township in northern Mengla County, and it matters because four of the old tea mountains fall inside it: Yibang, Mangzhi, Gedeng and Manzhuan. It is less a single tea than a place that holds several.

The tea is made in the raw pu-erh way, so differences come mainly from mountain and tree. Yibang is described as more showy in aroma than Gedeng.

In the cup, Gedeng is described as restrained, with honey and wild flowers and a slight bitterness that fades quickly into a long sweetness. These accounts come largely from tea writers and sellers, so taste for yourself.

When buying, look for the mountain and harvest season, not just the word Xiangming. Old trees are limited in these gardens, so ask how a seller knows where the leaf came from.
history:
The Ancient Tea Horse Road passed through the Xiangming area, and its four mountains belong to the old tea-mountain tradition of Xishuangbanna. One account says Gedeng's gardens peaked in the Qianlong era, reaching west to Mangzhi, before clashes destroyed much of them.

Today the township is linking tea with tourism: gardens interplanted with valuable trees, walking paths, restored villages and guesthouses run by tea families.
